what: Korea Electric Power, known as KEPCO, generates and distributes nearly all of South Korea's electricity. It is majority state-owned and the government sets the tariffs it may charge.
customers: Every household and business in South Korea, which has no alternative supplier.
money: generation and distribution across South Korea
moat: A national monopoly on transmission and distribution in an advanced economy, with nuclear and coal generation that no competitor could build.
risks: $89.9B of debt, accumulated when the government froze tariffs below fuel costs
The government, not the company, decides what it may charge, and tariff decisions are political
Free cash flow is negative by $1.5B because capital spending outruns earnings
opportunities: 3.1 times earnings, among the lowest valuations of any large utility anywhere
Revenue grew from $50.5B to $72.6B in four years as tariffs were finally raised
Back to profit at $3.7B of net income after the losses of the energy crisis years
watch: Tariff decisions by the Korean government and the pace of debt reduction.
